# RealityView + RealityKit on macOS 26 — 3D Device Viewer Build Guide

Research target: macOS 26 / Xcode 26 / Swift 6, SwiftUI `RealityView` hosting a Blender-authored USDZ. Every API below was checked against Apple's documentation JSON (the human-facing pages are JS SPAs and return empty to fetchers; the `/tutorials/data/...json` endpoints carry the real content).

**Legend**
- **[DOC]** = verified from the cited Apple documentation (signature + availability read from the doc JSON).
- **[REC]** = my recommendation / synthesis / known-community gotcha, not a direct doc quote.

**Availability cheat-sheet (all [DOC], read from each symbol's JSON):**

| API | min macOS | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `RealityView` | 15.0 | iOS 18, Catalyst 18, tvOS 26, visionOS 1 |
| `Entity(named:in:)` async / `Entity(contentsOf:withName:)` async | 15.0 | iOS 18 |
| `findEntity(named:)` | 10.15 | old API, recursive |
| `MeshResource.generate*` (box/sphere/cyl/cone/plane) | 10.15 | old API |
| `SimpleMaterial` | 10.15 | `PhysicallyBasedMaterial` = 12.0 |
| `DirectionalLightComponent` / `PointLightComponent` | 10.15 | `.Shadow` subcomponent |
| `ImageBasedLightComponent` (+Receiver) | 15.0 | IBL as an entity component |
| `GroundingShadowComponent` | 15.0 | contact shadow |
| `OrthographicCameraComponent` / `PerspectiveCameraComponent` | 15.0 | visionOS 2.0 |
| `.realityViewCameraControls(_:)` | 15.0 | `CameraControls.orbit/.tilt/.pan/.dolly` |
| `targetedToAnyEntity()` / `InputTargetComponent` | 15.0 | SwiftUI gesture → entity |
| `move(to:relativeTo:duration:timingFunction:)` | 10.15-era | returns `AnimationPlaybackController` |
| **`Entity.animate(_:body:)` / `content.animate {}`** | **26.0** | **NEW this cycle — implicit animation** |

The big macOS-26-specific finding: the **implicit animation API** (`Entity.animate`, `RealityViewContent.animate`) is brand-new at 26.0, and it's the one Apple's current "Automatically animating RealityKit entities" article is built around. Everything else your viewer needs already existed at macOS 15, so on macOS 26 you have the full surface.

---

## 1. `RealityView` on macOS — make/update model + loading

**[DOC]** `RealityView` is available **macOS 15.0+**. The initializer shape **differs by platform**, and this is the single most important macOS gotcha:

- On **visionOS**, the closures receive `inout RealityViewContent` and there are `attachments:` and `placeholder:` overloads.
- On **iOS / iPadOS / macOS / Mac Catalyst / tvOS**, the closures receive **`inout RealityViewCameraContent`** (a camera-backed content type), and only `init(make:update:)` and `init(make:update:placeholder:)` exist — **no `attachments:` initializer on macOS.**

Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/realityview

```swift
import SwiftUI
import RealityKit

struct DeviceViewer: View {
    @State private var model: Entity?

    var body: some View {
        RealityView { content in                 // make: (inout RealityViewCameraContent) async -> Void
            // Runs once. Async — you can await loads directly here.
            if let device = try? await Entity(named: "DeviceModel", in: .main) {
                content.add(device)
                model = device
            }
            content.add(makeLighting())          // see §4
            content.add(makeCamera())            // see §5
        } update: { content in                   // update: (inout RealityViewCameraContent) -> Void
            // Runs on every SwiftUI state change. Keep it cheap & idempotent.
            // Do NOT reload the model here. Reflect @State into entities only.
        }
        .realityViewCameraControls(.orbit)       // see §5
    }
}
```

**[DOC] Loading a bundled USDZ.** `convenience init(named:in:) async throws` returns the **root entity** of the file; `name` omits the extension; `bundle: nil` searches the main bundle. RealityKit loads `.usd/.usda/.usdc/.usdz` and `.reality`. There is also `init(contentsOf:withName:) async throws` for a file `URL`.
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/entity/init(named:in:)

**[REC]** Because `make` is `async`, `await` the load right inside it — that's the sanctioned pattern; use the `placeholder:` overload if you want a spinner while it loads. Don't kick loading off in `update`. If you need cancellable/parallel loads, use a `TaskGroup` inside `make` (the doc explicitly notes awaiting all loads before adding "to display content from multiple scenes without hitches or pop-in").

**[REC]** `ModelEntity(named:in:)` (subclass) is fine when you specifically need a `ModelComponent`/physics on the root, but `Entity(named:)` is correct for a hierarchical device model whose parts you'll look up by name.

## 2. Entity name resolution + a validation pass

**[DOC]** `func findEntity(named:) -> Entity?` performs a **depth-first recursive** search over all descendants and returns the **first** match. Verbatim: *"Entity names need not be unique."* Available macOS 10.15+.
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/entity/findentity(named:)

**[DOC/REC] USD prim → `Entity.name` mapping.** RealityKit sets each `Entity.name` from the USD prim name during load, and preserves the prim hierarchy as the entity tree. So a Blender object exported as prim `PowerButton` resolves via `root.findEntity(named: "PowerButton")`. Caveats you should design around ([REC], well-known behavior):
- Blender/USD **sanitizes** names to valid prim identifiers — spaces/dots/hyphens become `_`. "Power Button" → `Power_Button`. Validate against the *exported* names, not your Blender outliner names.
- Names are **not guaranteed unique**; `findEntity` returns only the first. For pads/buttons that repeat, give each a unique prim name in Blender or walk children explicitly.
- A mesh may be nested under an Xform prim of the same base name; the entity you get back may be the Xform, with the `ModelComponent` on a child. Don't assume the found entity holds the mesh.

**[REC] Validation pass** — assert the required contract at load and log misses:

```swift
enum RequiredNode: String, CaseIterable {
    case body = "DeviceBody"
    case screen = "Screen"
    case powerButton = "PowerButton"
    case volUp = "VolumeUp"
    case volDown = "VolumeDown"
}

@discardableResult
func validate(_ root: Entity) -> [RequiredNode: Entity] {
    var resolved: [RequiredNode: Entity] = [:]
    var missing: [String] = []
    for node in RequiredNode.allCases {
        if let e = root.findEntity(named: node.rawValue) {
            resolved[node] = e
        } else {
            missing.append(node.rawValue)
        }
    }
    if !missing.isEmpty {
        assertionFailure("USDZ missing required prims: \(missing.joined(separator: ", "))")
        // In release, downgrade to os.Logger .fault and fall back to §8 procedural model.
    }
    return resolved
}
```

**[REC]** To debug name mismatches, dump the tree once: recurse printing `entity.name` + component types. This is the fastest way to reconcile Blender export names with what RealityKit actually created.

## 3. Materials in code (override baked USDZ materials)

**[DOC] `PhysicallyBasedMaterial`** (macOS 12.0+) — the PBR material you want for a device. Properties are wrapper structs, not raw scalars:
- `baseColor: BaseColor` → `BaseColor(tint:texture:)`
- `roughness: Roughness` → `Roughness(scalar:)` (or floatLiteral)
- `metallic: Metallic` → `Metallic(scalar:)`
- `emissiveColor: EmissiveColor` (`EmissiveColor(tint:)`) + `emissiveIntensity: Float`

Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/physicallybasedmaterial

**[DOC] `SimpleMaterial`** (macOS 10.15+) — `SimpleMaterial(color:roughness:isMetallic:)`. Lighter, fewer knobs. Abstract: *"A basic material that responds to lights in the scene."*
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/simplematerial

```swift
func applyBrushedAluminum(to entity: Entity) {
    guard var model = entity.components[ModelComponent.self] else { return }
    var mat = PhysicallyBasedMaterial()
    mat.baseColor = .init(tint: .init(white: 0.72, alpha: 1))
    mat.roughness = .init(floatLiteral: 0.35)
    mat.metallic  = .init(floatLiteral: 1.0)
    // Override every material slot the mesh expects:
    model.materials = Array(repeating: mat, count: model.mesh.expectedMaterialCount)
    entity.components.set(model)          // reassign — components are value types
}
```

**[DOC/REC] Overriding baked materials.** The USDZ arrives with materials already on each `ModelComponent`. To replace them, read the component, rewrite `model.materials`, and **set it back** (RealityKit components are value types — mutating a copy does nothing until you `components.set`). Use `mesh.expectedMaterialCount` (a documented `MeshResource` property) to size the array so multi-submesh parts don't render untextured.

**[REC]** For an emissive screen "on" state, drive `emissiveIntensity` — and note (§7) it's animatable via the implicit API since `ModelComponent` is in the animatable set.

## 4. Lighting (key / fill / rim + IBL + grounding shadow)

RealityKit lights are **entity components** (there is no scene-level light list). Add a light component to an `Entity`, position/orient the entity, add it to content.

**[DOC] `DirectionalLightComponent`** (macOS 10.15+): `intensity: Float` (**lumen/m² = lux**), `color`, `isRealWorldProxy`. Enable shadows by also adding `DirectionalLightComponent.Shadow()`.
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/directionallightcomponent

```swift
let light = DirectionalLightComponent(color: .white, intensity: 10_000)
lightEntity.components.set([light, DirectionalLightComponent.Shadow()])
```

**[DOC] `ImageBasedLightComponent`** (macOS 15.0+): `init(source:intensityExponent:)`, plus `inheritsRotation`. `intensityExponent` multiplies base intensity by `2^exponent`. You attach the IBL to one entity and mark lit entities with **`ImageBasedLightReceiverComponent`**. Source (`ImageBasedLightComponent.Source`) is built from an `EnvironmentResource`.
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/imagebasedlightcomponent

**[DOC] `GroundingShadowComponent`** (macOS 15.0+): `GroundingShadowComponent(castsShadow: true, receivesShadow:)` — the soft contact shadow that makes a device look seated on a surface. Attach to the model entity.
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/groundingshadowcomponent

**[REC] A soft 3-point hero rig** ([DOC] for each component's existence/params; the *arrangement* is my recommendation):

```swift
func makeLighting() -> Entity {
    let rig = Entity()

    func dirLight(_ intensity: Float, _ dir: SIMD3<Float>, shadow: Bool) -> Entity {
        let e = Entity()
        var comps: [any Component] = [DirectionalLightComponent(color: .white, intensity: intensity)]
        if shadow { comps.append(DirectionalLightComponent.Shadow()) }
        e.components.set(comps)
        e.look(at: .zero, from: -dir, relativeTo: nil)   // aim toward origin
        return e
    }
    rig.addChild(dirLight(6_000, [ -0.5, -1, -0.6], shadow: true))  // key, upper-left
    rig.addChild(dirLight(2_000, [  0.8, -0.2, -0.4], shadow: false)) // fill, softer
    rig.addChild(dirLight(3_500, [  0.0,  0.3,  1.0], shadow: false)) // rim, from behind

    // IBL for realistic metal reflections (needs an EnvironmentResource, e.g. "studio.exr"→.usdz probe)
    if let env = try? EnvironmentResource.load(named: "studio") {
        let ibl = Entity()
        ibl.components.set(ImageBasedLightComponent(source: .single(env), intensityExponent: 0.6))
        rig.addChild(ibl)
        // Every device part entity should also get ImageBasedLightReceiverComponent(imageBasedLight: ibl)
    }
    return rig
}
```

**[REC]** Directional light intensity is in **lux**, so realistic values are in the thousands, not 0–1. Metals look dead without IBL — pair `metallic ≈ 1` (§3) with an `ImageBasedLightComponent` or the reflections have nothing to sample.

## 5. Camera — fixed near-ortho hero view + constrained orbit

**[DOC]** On macOS, `RealityView`'s content is **`RealityViewCameraContent`**, which exposes `camera: RealityViewCamera`, `cameraTarget: Entity?`, and (per its overview) *"coordinate conversions such as projections and raycasts."*
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/realityviewcameracontent

**[DOC] Camera entities.** Add either `PerspectiveCameraComponent` or `OrthographicCameraComponent` (both macOS 15.0+) to an entity. `OrthographicCameraComponent` has `scale`, `scaleDirection`, `near`, `far` and renders **without perspective** (far objects don't shrink) — exactly a "hero" isometric look. The doc's own example uses `look(at:from:relativeTo:)`:
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/orthographiccameracomponent

```swift
func makeCamera() -> Entity {
    let cam = Entity()
    var ortho = OrthographicCameraComponent()
    ortho.scale = 0.25              // smaller = more zoomed-in
    cam.components.set(ortho)
    cam.look(at: .zero, from: [0.6, 0.5, 1.0], relativeTo: nil)  // 3/4 hero angle
    return cam
}
```

**[REC]** For a "near-orthographic" look that still gives a touch of depth, use `PerspectiveCameraComponent` with a **small field of view** instead — true ortho can feel flat for a device shell. Pick one; both are one component swap.

**[DOC] Built-in orbit control.** `.realityViewCameraControls(_:)` (macOS 15.0+) adds drag-to-move-camera. `CameraControls` cases: **`.orbit`, `.tilt`, `.pan`, `.dolly`**. Verbatim: *"You can use a drag gesture from a mouse, trackpad, or screen touches … to `.tilt`, `.pan`, `.orbit`, or `.dolly` a virtual camera."*
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/realityviewcameracontrols(_:)

**[REC] Constraining yaw/pitch — important caveat.** `CameraControls.orbit` is a **fixed built-in** with **no exposed yaw/pitch clamp**. There is no documented API to limit its range, and forums report target-tracking quirks mid-interaction. If your brief truly requires clamped orbit, **don't use `.realityViewCameraControls`** — drive your own camera entity from a SwiftUI `DragGesture`, accumulate yaw/pitch, `.clamp` them, and rebuild the camera transform each frame:

```swift
@State private var yaw: Float = 0, pitch: Float = 0.3

// in a DragGesture .onChanged, then in update: reposition the camera entity
func orbitTransform(radius: Float) -> Transform {
    let clampedPitch = max(-0.4, min(0.8, pitch))          // limit tilt
    let clampedYaw   = max(-.pi/3, min(.pi/3, yaw))         // limit spin ±60°
    let x = radius * cos(clampedPitch) * sin(clampedYaw)
    let y = radius * sin(clampedPitch)
    let z = radius * cos(clampedPitch) * cos(clampedYaw)
    var t = Transform(); t.translation = [x, y, z]
    return t   // then camera.look(at:.zero, from: t.translation, relativeTo: nil)
}
```

This is the reliable path for a *constrained* hero viewer; the built-in modifier is the quick path for *unconstrained* orbit.

## 6. Hit testing & gestures (SwiftUI tap/drag → entity)

**[DOC] The macOS-15+ way is SwiftUI gestures targeted at entities.** `func targetedToAnyEntity() -> some Gesture<EntityTargetValue<Value>>` (macOS 15.0+). The gesture value is an **`EntityTargetValue`** exposing `.entity` (the hit entity) and coordinate-conversion helpers. Related: `targetedToEntity(_:)`, `targetedToEntity(where:)`.
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/gesture/targetedtoanyentity()

**[DOC] Requirement:** the entity must carry an **`InputTargetComponent`** (macOS 15.0+) **and** a **`CollisionComponent`** that defines the hit shape. `InputTargetComponent` is hierarchical and uses descendants' collision shapes.
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/inputtargetcomponent

```swift
// 1. Make each pad/button pickable at load:
func makePickable(_ e: Entity) {
    e.components.set(InputTargetComponent())
    let bounds = e.visualBounds(relativeTo: e)
    e.components.set(CollisionComponent(shapes: [.generateBox(size: bounds.extents)]))
}

// 2. Attach the gesture to the RealityView:
RealityView { content in /* … */ }
    .gesture(
        SpatialTapGesture()
            .targetedToAnyEntity()
            .onEnded { value in
                let tapped = value.entity              // [DOC] .entity
                press(tapped)                          // → §7 animate travel
            }
    )
```

**[REC]** `content` on macOS also advertises raycast/projection helpers (its overview mentions projections and raycasts), but the **gesture + `InputTargetComponent`/`CollisionComponent`** route is the documented, ergonomic one for tap/drag picking — prefer it over manual raycasting. Generate collision shapes from `visualBounds` at load rather than by hand; regenerate if you swap the mesh.

## 7. Animating transforms (key travel) at 60 Hz without SwiftUI churn

Two documented routes. For a device viewer, **avoid** re-rendering SwiftUI every frame — animate in RealityKit directly.

**[DOC] A. `move(to:relativeTo:duration:timingFunction:)`** — explicit, returns an **`AnimationPlaybackController`** you can track/stop. Ideal for a discrete button-press offset. Long-standing API (RealityKit 2 era).
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/entity/move(to:relativeto:duration:timingfunction:)-905k

```swift
func press(_ button: Entity) {
    var down = button.transform
    down.translation.y -= 0.0015                       // 1.5 mm of travel
    let ctrl = button.move(to: down, relativeTo: button.parent,
                           duration: 0.06, timingFunction: .easeOut)
    _ = ctrl                                            // hold if you need completion tracking

    // release back after the press bottoms out:
    DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + 0.06) {
        button.move(to: button.transform /* original */, relativeTo: button.parent,
                    duration: 0.08, timingFunction: .easeInOut)
    }
}
```

**[DOC] B. Implicit animation — NEW at macOS 26.0.** `static func Entity.animate(_:body:completion:)` and `RealityViewContent.animate(body:completion:)`. You set the end state inside the closure and RealityKit tweens it. Animatable components include **Transform, OpacityComponent, ModelComponent, DirectionalLightComponent, PointLightComponent, SpotLightComponent, ParticleEmitterComponent, BillboardComponent**. Both take an optional `completion`.
Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/automatically-animating-realitykit-entities and https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/entity/animate(_:body:completion:)

```swift
// macOS 26+ only — guard it:
if #available(macOS 26.0, *) {
    Entity.animate(.easeOut(duration: 0.06)) {
        button.components[Transform.self]?.translation.y -= 0.0015
    } completion: {
        Entity.animate(.easeInOut(duration: 0.08)) {
            button.components[Transform.self]?.translation.y += 0.0015
        }
    }
}
```

**[DOC] Critical rule** from the article: set Transform sub-properties **together through `entity.components[Transform.self]`**, not `position`/`scale`/`orientation` individually, or you get conflicting animations.

**[REC] For your use case:** use **`move(to:)`** (option A) for button travel — it works on every supported OS (not gated to 26), gives you a controller, and is the natural fit for a one-shot mechanical offset. Reserve the implicit API for macOS-26-only polish. For truly per-frame custom motion, subscribe once to `SceneEvents.Update` via `content.subscribe(to:)` and mutate transforms in the callback — this runs on RealityKit's render loop at display rate and **never touches SwiftUI `@State`**, which is exactly how you avoid per-frame view invalidation.

## 8. Procedural fallback via `MeshResource`

**[DOC]** `MeshResource` generators (macOS 10.15+ for the core set):
- `generateBox(size:cornerRadius:)` and `generateBox(width:height:depth:cornerRadius:splitFaces:)` — **rounded box via `cornerRadius`**, `splitFaces` for per-face materials.
- `generateSphere(radius:)`, `generateCylinder(height:radius:)`, `generateCone(height:radius:)`, `generatePlane(width:height:cornerRadius:)` / `generatePlane(width:depth:cornerRadius:)`, `generateText(...)`.
- Custom geometry: `generate(from: MeshResource.Contents)` (throwing). Instancing via `MeshResource.Instance` (transform a `Model` to a location) inside `Contents`.

Source: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/realitykit/meshresource

```swift
func placeholderDevice() -> Entity {
    let root = Entity()

    let bodyMesh = MeshResource.generateBox(width: 0.07, height: 0.005, depth: 0.14, cornerRadius: 0.004, splitFaces: false)
    let body = ModelEntity(mesh: bodyMesh,
                           materials: [SimpleMaterial(color: .darkGray, roughness: 0.4, isMetallic: true)])
    body.name = "DeviceBody"
    root.addChild(body)

    // Cylindrical buttons, instanced by position:
    for (name, x) in [("VolumeUp", -0.036), ("VolumeDown", -0.036), ("PowerButton", 0.036)] {
        let btn = ModelEntity(mesh: .generateCylinder(height: 0.006, radius: 0.003),
                              materials: [SimpleMaterial(color: .lightGray, roughness: 0.3, isMetallic: true)])
        btn.name = name
        btn.orientation = simd_quatf(angle: .pi/2, axis: [0,0,1])   // lay on its side
        btn.position = [Float(x), 0.0, 0.05]
        root.addChild(btn)
    }
    return root
}
```

**[REC]** Give procedural parts the **same names** your validation contract (§2) expects, so the rest of the app (§3 materials, §6 picking, §7 travel) works identically whether the real USDZ loaded or you fell back. `generateBox(...cornerRadius:)` is genuinely the right primitive for a phone/remote shell; use `generateCylinder` for round buttons and `generatePlane` for the screen quad.

## 9. Pitfalls (macOS 26 / USDZ / scale / perf)

**[DOC-backed]**
- **Platform closure type differs.** macOS/iOS `make`/`update` take `inout RealityViewCameraContent`; visionOS takes `inout RealityViewContent`. **No `attachments:` initializer on macOS** — SwiftUI-in-3D attachments are visionOS-only. Copying a visionOS sample verbatim will not compile on macOS.
- **`Entity.animate` is 26.0-only.** Gate with `#available(macOS 26.0, *)` or use `move(to:)`. Same for anything else you pull from the "Automatically animating…" article.
- **Camera components / IBL / grounding shadow / gesture targeting are macOS 15.0+**, so fine on 26 but they won't back-deploy to macOS 14. `findEntity`, `MeshResource.generate*`, `SimpleMaterial`, `DirectionalLightComponent` go back to 10.15 — mixing old + new means your `@available` floor is effectively **15.0 (or 26.0 if you use implicit animation)**.

**[REC] — coordinate / scale / naming**
- **Units are meters.** RealityKit and USD are metric; a device modeled at "70 mm" must be `0.07`. If your Blender scene used centimeters/arbitrary units, the model will import 100× too big/small. Check `entity.visualBounds` right after load and rescale the root if needed.
- **Blender is Z-up; USD/RealityKit are Y-up.** Blender's USD exporter converts axes, but a mis-set "Convert Orientation"/up-axis on export lands the device on its side or back. If parts look rotated 90°, it's the export axis, not your code.
- **Prim-name sanitization** (see §2): spaces/dots → `_`. Validate against exported names.
- **Baked vs. code materials:** setting `model.materials` requires reading the component, mutating, and `components.set` back (value semantics). Forgetting the write-back is the #1 "my color didn't change" bug. Size arrays with `mesh.expectedMaterialCount`.
- **Non-unique names** make `findEntity` return the wrong twin; give repeated pads unique prim names in Blender.

**[REC] — performance**
- **Never reload in `update`.** Load once in `make`; `update` should only reflect state. Reloading per state change causes pop-in and leaks.
- **Animate on RealityKit's loop, not SwiftUI's.** Use `move(to:)`/implicit-animate/`SceneEvents.Update` subscription for the 60 Hz key travel; keep `@State` out of the hot path so SwiftUI doesn't re-diff the view tree each frame.
- **Collision shapes:** use one cheap generated box/sphere per pickable part (§6); don't turn on convex mesh collision for the whole device — hit-testing a fixed hero view doesn't need it and it's costly to generate.
- **One IBL, shared:** attach a single `ImageBasedLightComponent` and mark parts as receivers rather than lighting each part separately.
